text: Severin Roesen was born in Boppard in Prussia, and little is known about his early life or education. He worked as a porcelain painter in Cologne and exhibited a floral painting at the local art club in 1847. That same year he married Sophia Lambricht. They sailed to England and from there emigrated to New York. He became known for abundant fruit and flower still lifes. Today he is recognized as one of the major American painters in that genre in the nineteenth century.

Alphonse Osbert was educated at the École des Beaux-Arts, but his first passion was for the great Spanish masters, especially Jusepe de Ribera. In the late 1880s he moved away from his academic style. He gave up naturalistic painting for a Pointillist technique like the one used by Seurat and Signac. Pierre Puvis de Chavannes and the Symbolists inspired him as well. He stopped depicting real-world subjects and developed a poetic visual language of his own. His signature style shows ghostlike Muses in mysterious landscapes under the unearthly light of a sun or moon.

Francesco Pesellino got his nickname from his grandfather, the painter Giuliano Pesello. His own father, also a painter, died when Francesco was a child. He went to live with his grandfather and became his pupil. He stayed in the studio until the old man's death, then formed working partnerships with other artists, such as Zanobi Strozzi and Fra Filippo Lippi. In the following years he made his reputation with small, highly finished works for domestic interiors. He died in his mid-thirties.

Gabriel François Doyen's father was a royal upholsterer who first opposed his wish to become an artist. At twelve he began taking lessons from Charles-André van Loo. He made rapid progress and won the Grand Prix de Rome at twenty. In 1748 he set out for Italy and travelled throughout the country, studying the works of Domenichino, Annibale Carracci, Pietro da Cortona, Giulio Romano and Michelangelo. In Venice he was greatly influenced by colourists such as Titian. He painted historical and mythological scenes.

Jan van Noordt was one of four sons of a schoolteacher and carillonneur. The family came from Schagen in North Holland and moved to Amsterdam in the late 1630s. His brothers Jacobus and Anthonie became the most prominent organists in the city, with posts in churches including the Oude Kerk. Jan trained under Jacob Adriaensz. Backer, and he was already contributing to paintings in 1640. One of them is David and Bathsheba, now in a private collection in Tokyo.

Wilhelm von Wright was born in Haminalahti in Kuopio, Finland, on his father's family estate. His brothers Magnus and Ferdinand became painters and illustrators too. At Magnus's invitation he travelled to Sweden at 13 and helped produce the multi-volume Svenska Fåglar for the ornithologist Nils Bonde. His most important solo effort was Skandinaviens fiskar. He was a painter and an amateur naturalist.

Bartolomeo Montagna was born Bartolomeo Cincani and later changed his name. He worked mainly in Vicenza, and also in Venice, Verona and Padua. He is most famous for his many Madonnas. His figures are soft, and his pictures often show eccentric marble architecture. Giovanni Bellini influenced him heavily, and he might have worked in Bellini's workshop around 1470. Vasari called him a student of Andrea Mantegna, but art historians widely contest that. His son Benedetto was a productive engraver.

Salomon Gessner's father was a printer and publisher in Zürich. In 1749 Gessner began an apprenticeship at a Berlin bookshop but stayed only a year, because he had decided to devote himself to landscape painting and etching. After a short stay in Hamburg he encountered the poetic works of Karl Wilhelm Ramler and Friedrich von Hagedorn. He became a poet, best known for his Idylls. He also co-founded the Helvetic Society and was the first publisher and editor of the Neue Zürcher Zeitung.
